<problem>
Let \(g\geq2\) be an integer, and set
\[
r=\left\lfloor\frac{g+2}{3}\right\rfloor,\qquad k=g-r.
\]
Let \(C_g\) be the smooth projective completion over \(\mathbb C\) of the affine curve
\[
z^2=x^{2g+1}-1,
\]
and let \(p\) be its unique point over infinity. Choose the local parameter \(t\) at \(p\) satisfying
\[
x=t^{-2},\qquad z=t^{-(2g+1)}(1-t^{4g+2})^{1/2},
\]
where the square root has value \(1\) at \(t=0\).

For a nonzero vector \(b=(b_0,\ldots,b_{r-1})\in\mathbb C^r\), define
\[
\phi_b(t)=\sum_{j=0}^{r-1}b_jt^{-(2g-1-2j)}.
\]
Choose coordinate discs \(W_0\Subset W\) centered at \(p\), with \(t\) defined on a neighborhood of \(\overline W\), and put \(U=C_g\setminus\overline{W_0}\). Take product neighborhoods of the zero sections over \(U\) and \(W\), with fiber coordinates \(y_U\) and \(y_W\). After shrinking the fiber directions, glue them over \(U\cap W\), preserving the base point, by
\[
y_W=t^{-1}y_U\bigl(1+k\phi_b(t)y_U^k\bigr)^{-1/k}.
\]
The fractional power denotes the holomorphic branch whose value is \(1\) at \(y_U=0\).

Let \(X_b\) be the resulting smooth analytic surface germ along its zero section \(E\simeq C_g\). Its normal bundle is \(\mathcal O_{C_g}(-p)\), and contracting \(E\) gives a normal surface singularity \((V_b,0)\) with minimal good resolution \(f_b:(X_b,E)\to(V_b,0)\). For cohomology, take \(X_b\) to be the inverse image of a sufficiently small Stein representative of this singularity.

Write \(\mathcal I_E\) for the ideal sheaf of \(E\), and define the logarithmic tangent sheaf by
\[
S_b=\{D\in\Theta_{X_b}:D(\mathcal I_E)\subseteq\mathcal I_E\},
\]
where \(\Theta_{X_b}\) is the sheaf of holomorphic vector fields. Put \(L_b=\bigwedge^2S_b\) and \(h^1(X_b,\mathcal F)=\dim_{\mathbb C}H^1(X_b,\mathcal F)\). Determine the exact formula, as a function of \(g\) and the entire coefficient vector \(b\), for
\[
\Delta_b=h^1(X_b,\mathcal O_{X_b})-h^1(X_b,S_b)+h^1(X_b,L_b),
\]
for every allowed nonzero \(b\), including vectors with vanishing components.
</problem>

A complete answer to this problem: A complete answer is an exact formula or fully specified finite computation for the single integer Δ_b as a function of every integer g ≥ 2 and every nonzero coefficient vector b ∈ ℂ^r, where r = floor((g+2)/3). It must cover all allowed coefficient patterns, including vanishing components, with any case distinctions explicitly and exhaustively specified.

55	## 2. The logarithmic tangent sequence

133	D\left(f(u)\,u\frac{\partial}{\partial u}\right)
134	=u f'(u)-kf(u).                                         \tag{13}
135	\]

200	## 4. The remaining obstruction has rank \(m+1\)
201	
202	A basis of \(H^0(C,\mathcal O_C(kp))\) is
203	\[
204	1,x,\ldots,x^{\lfloor k/2\rfloor}.
205	\]

207	\[
208	f\longmapsto[\phi f]\in H^1(C,\mathcal O_C(2kp)).        \tag{20}
209	\]

211	The gaps greater than \(2k\) are exactly
212	\[
213	q_j=2g-1-2j,\qquad 0\le j<r.
214	\]
215	For the source vector \(x^a=t^{-2a}\), the coefficient of \(t^{-q_j}\) in \(\phi x^a\) is
216	\[
217	M_{j,a}=b_{j+a},                                        \tag{21}
218	\]
219	where \(b_\ell=0\) for \(\ell>m\).
220	
221	Because \(k\ge2r-2\), the matrix contains its first \(m+1\) columns. Its first \((m+1)\)-square block is anti-triangular, with anti-diagonal \(b_m\), so
222	\[
223	\det(M_{j,a})_{0\le j,a\le m}
224	=(-1)^{m(m+1)/2}b_m^{m+1}\ne0.                          \tag{22}
225	\]
226	Every column \(a>m\) vanishes. Hence the first obstruction has rank \(m+1\), and its kernel is exactly
227	\[
228	\operatorname{span}\{x^a:m<a\le\lfloor k/2\rfloor\}.     \tag{23}
229	\]
230	
231	We must check that this kernel has no later obstruction.
232	
233	For \(a>m\), every term of \(\phi x^a\) has odd pole
234	\[
235	2g-1-2j+2a=2g+1+2(a-j-1).
236	\]

247	4g+2-(2g-1-2j+2a)>0.
248	\]
249	Thus the first correction can be chosen odd under \(t\mapsto-t\).

251	The next obstruction, in degree \(3k\), is even: it consists of terms involving either \(\phi^2x^a\) or \(\phi\) times this odd correction. All classes in (1) are odd, so this obstruction vanishes.

253	Finally, \(3k\ge d\) and \(4k>d\). Therefore:

259	\[
